claim: The dorsal funiculus in the spinal cord relays somatosensory information to the brain.
source: The dorsal funiculus in the spinal cord relays somatosensory information to the brain.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the function of the dorsal funiculus in the spinal cord.

claim: The dorsal funiculus is made of T-shaped bifurcation of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) sensory axons.
source: It is made of T-shaped bifurcation of dorsal root ganglion (DRG) sensory axons.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the anatomical structure of the dorsal funiculus.

claim: Slit signaling is required for proper guidance during bifurcation.
source: Our previous study has shown that Slit signaling is required for proper guidance during bifurcation
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Loss of Slit does not affect all DRG axons.
source: but loss of Slit does not affect all DRG axons
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work showing incomplete penetrance of the Slit phenotype.

claim: Mice lacking Ntn1 had axons escaping from the dorsal funiculus at the time of bifurcation.
source: Using wholemount staining with tissue clearing, we showed that mice lacking Ntn1 had axons escaping from the dorsal funiculus at the time of bifurcation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from wholemount staining and tissue clearing experiments shown in the manuscript.

claim: The misprojecting axons in Ntn1 mutants come from DRG neurons.
source: Genetic labeling confirmed that these misprojecting axons come from DRG neurons.
evidence: This is supported by genetic labeling experiments using Neurog1-CreERT2 and tdTomato reporter shown in Figure 2.

claim: Loss of Ntn1 did not affect bifurcation but rather altered turning angles.
source: Single axon analysis showed that loss of Ntn1 did not affect bifurcation but rather altered turning angles.
evidence: This is supported by single axon DiI labeling data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Mice with triple deletion of Ntn1, Slit1, and Slit2 have a completely disorganized dorsal funiculus.
source: we examined mice with triple deletion of Ntn1, Slit1, and Slit2 and found a completely disorganized dorsal funiculus
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from triple mutant analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Comparing mice with different genotypes revealed additive guidance errors, demonstrating the independent roles of Ntn1 and Slit.
source: Comparing mice with different genotypes using immunolabeling and single axon tracing revealed additive guidance errors, demonstrating the independent roles of Ntn1 and Slit.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of different mutant genotypes shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: The same defects were observed in embryos lacking the cognate receptors of Ntn1 and Slit.
source: Moreover, the same defects were observed in embryos lacking their cognate receptors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from receptor mutant analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: Multi-factorial guidance mechanisms ensure proper formation of T-shaped bifurcation during spinal cord development.
source: These in vivo studies thus demonstrate the presence of multi-factorial guidance mechanisms that ensure proper formation of a common branched axonal structure during spinal cord development.
evidence: This is inferred from the combined analysis of multiple mutants showing additive defects.

claim: DRG central projections relay somatosensory information collected by their peripheral projections in the skin and muscle to the brain.
source: These projections relay somatosensory information (e.g., pain and touch) collected by their peripheral projections in the skin and muscle to the brain
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on DRG function.

claim: DRG axons bifurcate in the dorsal root entry zone (DREZ) upon reaching the dorsal spinal cord.
source: Upon reaching the dorsal spinal cord, they normally bifurcate in a location called the dorsal root entry zone (DREZ
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on DRG axon development.

claim: The bifurcated branches extend in opposite directions along the rostrocaudal axis, generating T-shaped junctions.
source: The bifurcated branches appear to extend in opposite directions along the rostrocaudal axis, generating T-shaped junctions, as part of the dorsal funiculus in the DREZ
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and Figure 1E showing the structure.

claim: Damage to or malformation of the dorsal funiculus can lead to paralysis.
source: Damage to or malformation of this evolutionarily conserved axonal structure in the DREZ can lead to paralysis, as commonly seen after spinal cord injury or in genetic disorders such as Frederick ataxia
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on spinal cord injury and genetic disorders.

claim: In mice, DRG central projections reach the dorsal spinal cord at embryonic day (E) 10.5.
source: In mice, after reaching the dorsal spinal cord at embryonic day (E) 10.5
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on DRG axon development timing.

claim: DRG central projections generate a new branch in response to C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) present in the dorsal spinal cord.
source: the DRG central projection first generates a new branch in response to the C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP) present in the dorsal spinal cord
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on CNP signaling in DRG axon bifurcation.

claim: Branch formation requires the CNP receptor Npr2 as well as cGMP signaling.
source: a step that requires the CNP receptor Npr2 as well as cGMP signaling
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on CNP signaling mechanisms.

claim: Slit1 and Slit2 are expressed next to the DREZ inside the spinal cord.
source: Slit1 and Slit2, which are expressed next to the DREZ inside the spinal cord
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on Slit expression patterns.

claim: Robo receptors are expressed by DRG neurons.
source: as well as their Robo receptors, which are expressed by DRG neurons
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on Robo receptor expression.

claim: In mouse mutants lacking Slit1 and Slit2 or their receptors Robo1 and Robo2, one of the daughter branches misprojects into the spinal cord.
source: In mouse mutants lacking Slit1 and Slit2 or their receptors Robo1 and Robo2, one of the daughter branches misprojects into the spinal cord.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on Slit/Robo mutant phenotypes.

claim: The defect in Slit1/Slit2 mutants only affects ~50% DRG axons and does not eliminate the dorsal funiculus.
source: However, the defect only affects ~50% DRG axons and does not eliminate the dorsal funiculus
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work showing incomplete penetrance of the Slit phenotype.

claim: Netrin-1 (Ntn1) is an extracellular molecule expressed in the spinal cord.
source: we re-evaluated the role of Netrin-1 (Ntn1), an extracellular molecule expressed in the spinal cord
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B showing expression data.

claim: Early studies of Ntn1 deletion identified aberrant entry of sensory axons into the dorsal spinal cord at E11.5 and E12.5.
source: Early studies of Ntn1 deletion based on a gene-trap allele (Ntn1β/β) as well as targeted deletion alleles have identified aberrant entry of sensory axons into the dorsal spinal cord at E11.5 and E12.5
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple previous studies on Ntn1 mutant phenotypes.

claim: Ntn1 is expressed immediately adjacent to the DREZ at E11.5.
source: Because of its expression immediately adjacent to the DREZ at E11.5
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on Ntn1 expression patterns.

claim: It has been suggested that Ntn1 prevents premature ingrowth of sensory afferents into the spinal cord via repulsion.
source: it has been suggested that Ntn1 prevents premature ingrowth of sensory afferents into the spinal cord via repulsion, an activity that was demonstrated in vitro
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies on Ntn1 function.

claim: Ntn1 transcripts are found mainly confined to the inside of the spinal cord, including the floor plate, the ventricular zone, and the lateral domain in the dorsal horn below the dorsal funiculus along the pial layer from E10.5 to E11.5.
source: Ntn1 transcripts are found mainly confined to the inside of the spinal cord, including the floor plate, the ventricular zone, and the lateral domain in the dorsal horn below the dorsal funiculus along the pial layer from E10.5 to E11.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B arrows).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–B and is consistent with previous published expression data.

claim: Ntn1 proteins are made by ventricular zone neural progenitor cells and deposited along the pial layer adjacent to the DREZ.
source: This RNA expression profile is in line with the localization of Ntn1 proteins made by ventricular zone neural progenitor cells and deposited along the pial layer adjacent to the DREZ
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on Ntn1 protein localization.

claim: In wild type embryos, central DRG axons extend dorsally, enter the spinal cord, bundle and form the dorsal funiculus that runs along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: As shown in wild type (WT) embryos, the central DRG axons first extend dorsally, enter the spinal cord, bundle and form the dorsal funiculus that runs along the rostrocaudal axis (Figure 1A and C).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A and C.

claim: The dorsal funiculus is thicker near the forelimb than near the hindlimb due to developmental delay along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: Due to the developmental delay along the rostrocaudal axis, the dorsal funiculus shown as a longitudinal track is thicker near the forelimb (Figure 1A) than near the hindlimb (Figure 1C), where it has just begun to form from bifurcated axons.
evidence: This is inferred from the developmental timing and supported by images in Figure 1A and C showing different thicknesses.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutants, a subpopulation of NF-labeled fibers escape the dorsal funiculus tract.
source: However, while some axons remain in the tract, a subpopulation of NF-labeled fibers (Figure 1B arrows) were found to escape the tract, filling the space above the dorsal funiculus.
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Misprojecting fibers appear in the hindlimb region where the dorsal funiculus starts to emerge, suggesting that the defect happens at the time of bifurcation.
source: These misprojecting fiber can be seen in traditional NF staining (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E, F, I, J). They appear in the hindlimb region where the dorsal funiculus starts to emerge (Figure 1D), suggesting that the defect happens at the time of bifurcation.
evidence: This is inferred from the location and timing of misprojections shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutants, an average of 22 fibers per DRG were found in the line proximal to the DREZ, 17 fibers/DRG in the medial line, and 14 fibers/DRG in the distal line.
source: In Ntn1β/β mutants, an average of 22 fibers per DRG were found in the line proximal to the DREZ, 17 fibers/DRG were found in the medial line, and 14 fibers/DRG were found in the distal line that is closest to the midline (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of wholemount images shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The presence of NF-fibers in the dorsal midline of Ntn1 mutants suggests that misprojections climb up in the dorsal spinal cord.
source: The presence of NF-fibers in the dorsal midline of the Ntn1mutants suggests that misprojections climb up in the dorsal spinal cord.
evidence: This is inferred from the distribution of misprojections at different distances from the DREZ.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutants, NF-labeled fibers extended out from the DREZ at both E10.5 and E11.5.
source: However, in Ntn1β/β mutants, NF-labeled fibers extended out from the DREZ at both ages.
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 1K, L, M and N.

claim: More misprojections were found at E11.5 than E10.5, but they all grow along the pia surface.
source: More misprojections were found at E11.5, but they all grow along the pia surface (Figure 1K, L, M and N)
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 1K, L, M and N.

claim: Loss of Ntn1 caused NF-labeled axons to escape from the DREZ.
source: Thus, loss of Ntn1 caused NF-labeled axons to escape from the DREZ.
evidence: This is concluded from the wholemount and transverse section analysis showing misprojections in Ntn1 mutants.

claim: Neurog1-CreERT2 driver labels all DRG neurons.
source: We thus introduced a neural specific CreERT2 recombinase driver (Neurog1-CreERT2) and an Ai14 Cre reporter to our Ntn1 mice to label all DRG neurons
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on the Neurog1-CreERT2 driver and its use in labeling DRG neurons.

claim: In WT control embryos, tdTomato labeling is seen in DRG cell bodies, central axons projecting toward the dorsal spinal cord, and the dorsal funiculus.
source: In WT control embryos, tdTomato labeling is seen in DRG cell bodies (Figure 2A, asterisks), central axons projecting toward the dorsal spinal cord, and the dorsal funiculus (Figure 2A, yellow dotted box)
evidence: This is supported by genetic labeling data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutant embryos, tdTomato labeling is seen in DRG central projections as well as misprojections that escape from the DREZ and reach the dorsal spinal cord.
source: In Ntn1β/β mutant embryos, tdTomato labeling is seen in DRG central projections as well as misprojections that escape from the DREZ and reach the dorsal spinal cord (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is supported by genetic labeling data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: All tdTomato-labeled misprojections are NF-positive.
source: While not all NF misprojections are tdTomato positive, all tdTomato-labeled misprojections are NF-positive (Figure 2B").
evidence: This is supported by co-labeling analysis shown in Figure 2B".

claim: Most misprojecting fibers are stained for both tdTomato and NF.
source: This can be demonstrated by closer examination of the region above the DREZ (Figure 2C) where most misprojecting fibers are stained for both tdTomato and NF (Figure 2C", yellow arrows)
evidence: This is supported by co-labeling analysis shown in Figure 2C".

claim: tdTomato-labeled misprojections came directly from the DREZ.
source: Importantly, these tdTomato-labeled misprojections came directly from the DREZ (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by genetic labeling data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: D2 dorsal interneurons inside the spinal cord express Neurog1.
source: D2 dorsal interneurons inside the spinal cord are known to express Neurog1
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on Neurog1 expression in D2 interneurons.

claim: D2 interneurons are not labeled by NF and thus do not contribute to the NF-labeled misprojections.
source: Although they are labeled by tdTomato staining, D2 interneurons are not labeled by NF (see Figure 2A and A") and thus do not contribute to the NF-labeled misprojections.
evidence: This is supported by co-labeling analysis shown in Figure 2A and A".

claim: Neurog1-CreERT2 may not be active in all DRG neurons, so tdTomato-labeled misprojections likely underrepresent the DRG axon misprojections.
source: On the other hand, since Neurog1-CreERT2 may not be active in all DRG neurons, tdTomato-labeled misprojections likely underrepresent the DRG axon misprojections.
evidence: This is inferred from the known limitations of the Cre driver system.

claim: Some if not all NF-labeled misprojections are from DRG sensory neurons.
source: Thus, these data support that some if not all NF-labeled misprojections seen above are from DRG sensory neurons.
evidence: This is concluded from the genetic labeling experiments showing co-localization of tdTomato and NF in misprojections.

claim: In WT animals, bifurcated axons (n=11/12) and non-bifurcated axons (n=14/14) stay within the DREZ.
source: Normal turning is found in WT animals (n=3) for bifurcated (D, n=11/12 axons) and non-bifurcated axons (E, n=14/14 axons).
evidence: This is supported by sparse labeling data shown in Figure 2D, E, and I.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutants, ~55% bifurcated and ~70% non-bifurcated axons misprojected outside of the defined dorsal funiculus.
source: whereas ~55% bifurcated and ~70% non-bifurcated axons in the Ntn1β/β mutants misprojected outside of the defined dorsal funiculus (Figure 2I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of sparse labeling data shown in Figure 2I.

claim: Loss of Ntn1 alters the guidance of DRG axons at the DREZ during bifurcation.
source: These results demonstrate that loss of Ntn1 alters the guidance of DRG axons at the DREZ during bifurcation.
evidence: This is concluded from the sparse labeling experiments showing misprojections in Ntn1 mutants.

claim: Impaired Slit signaling led to misguidance of one of the bifurcated DRG branches, which enter the dorsal spinal cord in the absence of Slit/Robo signaling.
source: Our previous studies showed that impaired Slit signaling led to misguidance of one of the bifurcated DRG branches, which enter the dorsal spinal cord in the absence of Slit/Robo signaling
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on Slit/Robo mutant phenotypes.

claim: The misprojections in Ntn1 mutants appear on the dorsal pial surface and stay outside the spinal cord.
source: Since the misprojections in Ntn1 mutants appear on the dorsal pial surface and stay outside the spinal cord
evidence: This is supported by the transverse section analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ntn1 and Slit have different guidance functions that are both required for the formation of the dorsal funiculus.
source: we hypothesize that Ntn1 and Slit have different guidance functions that are both required for the formation of the dorsal funiculus.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the different phenotypes observed in Ntn1 and Slit mutants.

claim: Slit1 null background (Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1+/+) has nearly normal DRG axon projections.
source: Triple mutants were generated in the Slit1 null background (Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1+/+), which has nearly normal DRG axon projections (Figure 3A)
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: NF labeled axons are completely disorganized around the DREZ in triple mutants (Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1β/β).
source: In contrast, NF labeled axons are completely disorganized around the DREZ (dotted-line region) in triple mutants (Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1β/β) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both Slit and Ntn1 are needed for the formation and integrity of the dorsal funiculus.
source: This analysis of triple mutants demonstrates that both Slit and Ntn1 are needed for the formation and integrity of the dorsal funiculus
evidence: This is concluded from the severe disorganization observed in triple mutants.

claim: Slit and Ntn1 have different guidance roles during DRG axon bifurcation.
source: and supports the notion that they have different guidance roles during DRG axon bifurcation.
evidence: This is inferred from the different phenotypes observed in single and double mutants compared to triple mutants.

claim: In double mutants lacking both Slit1 and Slit2, an increased number of DRG axons leave the DREZ and appear in the proximal region of the dorsal spinal cord.
source: In double mutants lacking both Slit1 and Slit2 (Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1+/+), an increased number of DRG axons leave the DREZ (Figure 3E, arrows) and appear in the proximal region of the dorsal spinal cord (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Misprojections in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutants maintain a relatively straight trajectory perpendicular to the DREZ.
source: This can be demonstrated by viewing the misprojections from the dorsal side of the spinal cord (Figure 3K), as those misprojections maintain a relatively straight trajectory perpendicular to the DREZ.
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data viewed from the dorsal side shown in Figure 3K.

claim: Misprojections in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutants reach the midline but stop there without crossing to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.
source: They also reach the midline but stop there without crossing to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data viewed from the dorsal side shown in Figure 3K.

claim: NF-labeled fibers in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutants appear to enter the spinal cord from the DREZ with horizontal trajectories inside the dorsal proper.
source: Such a trajectory is consistent with their invasion into the spinal cord, which can be shown on the transverse-section of the spinal cord. There, NF-labeled fibers appear to enter the spinal cord from the DREZ with horizontal trajectories inside the dorsal proper (Figure 3Q, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 3Q.

claim: Misprojections in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutants reach the midline with an average length of 137.8 μm and a summed length of ~0.8 mm.
source: These misprojections reach the midline with an average length of 137.8 μm and a summed length of ~0.8 mm, indicating a high number of misprojections (Figure 3T).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transverse sections shown in Figure 3T.

claim: Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β embryos have a large number of dorsal misprojections that spread out in random directions from the DREZ along the dorsal spinal cord.
source: As in Ntn1 mutants, Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β embryos have a large number of dorsal misprojections that spread out in random directions from the DREZ along the dorsal spinal cord when viewed from the side (Figure 3F, arrowheads).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Misprojections in Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β embryos are wavy and long, sometimes passing the midline and reaching to the contralateral side of the spinal cord.
source: This can be corroborated by the dorsal view, which demonstrates that misprojections are wavy and long, sometimes passing the midline and reaching to the contralateral side of the spinal cord (Figure 3L).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data viewed from the dorsal side shown in Figure 3L.

claim: Misprojections in Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β embryos emerge from the DREZ and grow upward along the pial layer.
source: Such pattern is the result of misprojections emerging from the DREZ and growing upward along the pial layer as shown on the transverse section (Figure 3R).
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 3R.

claim: The distance from the midline to the DREZ is reduced to ~6 μm in Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β embryos from ~69 μm of the Slit1-/- control animal.
source: As a consequence, the distance from the midline to the DREZ is reduced to ~6 μm from ~69 μm of the Slit1-/- control animal (Figure 3T).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transverse sections shown in Figure 3T.

claim: Most misprojections in Slit1-/-;Slit2+/+;Ntn1β/β embryos stay outside the dorsal proper of the spinal cord.
source: Although there are similar total numbers of misprojections as those in the Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1+/+ animals (Figure 3T), most of them stay outside the dorsal proper of the spinal cord (Figure 3R)
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 3R and quantification in Figure 3T.

claim: The phenotype of triple mutants is more severe than that in Ntn1β/β mutants or Slit1;Slit2 double mutants.
source: As a result, the phenotype of triple mutants is more severe than that in Ntn1β/β mutants (Figure 1, Figure 3F) or Slit1;Slit2 double mutants (Figure 3E)
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figures 1 and 3.

claim: Triple mutants show an increase in dorsally oriented fibers extending at all three proximal-medial-distal locations between the DREZ and the roof plate.
source: which is demonstrated by an increase in these dorsally oriented fibers extending at all three proximal-medial-distal locations between the DREZ and the roof plate (Figure 3H).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of wholemount images shown in Figure 3H.

claim: In triple mutants, both straight and randomly oriented misprojections co-exist.
source: From the dorsal view, both straight and randomly oriented misprojections co-exist (Figure 3M)
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data viewed from the dorsal side shown in Figure 3M.

claim: In triple mutants, misprojections are found both inside the dorsal spinal cord and along the pial surface, demonstrating additive guidance errors when both signaling pathways are impaired.
source: and from the cross section, misprojections are found both inside the dorsal spinal cord and along the pial surface, demonstrating additive guidance errors when both signaling pathways are impaired (Figure 3H, N and T).
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 3N and quantification in Figure 3T.

claim: The distinct linear line in the DREZ appears uneven and often broken in triple mutants.
source: In addition, due to few axons turning into the DREZ, the distinct linear line in the DREZ appears uneven and often broken in the dorsal view (Figure 3M)
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data viewed from the dorsal side shown in Figure 3M.

claim: The DREZ became elongated in triple mutants.
source: and the DREZ became elongated in the transverse section (Figure 3S).
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 3S.

claim: Mice lacking Ntn1 and Slit1/2 have distinct phenotypes, supporting the different guidance roles of these pathways during dorsal funiculus development.
source: Taken together, these analyses from different views of the DREZ reveal distinct phenotypes in mice lacking Ntn1 and Slit1/2, thus supporting the different guidance roles of these pathways during dorsal funiculus development.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparative analysis of different mutant genotypes.

claim: In WT embryos, 26 out of 27 labeled axons have T-shaped junctions at the DREZ.
source: Indeed, in WT embryos, labeled axons properly turn at the DREZ and 26 out of 27 axons have T-shaped junctions at the DREZ (Figure 4B and D).
evidence: This is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 4B and D.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutants, 32 out of 34 axons analyzed have two branches.
source: In Ntn1β/β mutants, 32 out of 34 axons analyzed also have two branches (Figure 4F)
evidence: This is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Branch formation itself is not affected in the absence of Ntn1.
source: indicating that branch formation itself is not affected in the absence of Ntn1.
evidence: This is concluded from the DiI labeling data showing similar bifurcation rates in WT and Ntn1 mutants.

claim: In Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutant embryos, 28 out of 29 axons have bifurcated.
source: Similarly, 28 out of 29 axons have bifurcated in the Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutant embryos (Figure 4E)
evidence: This is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: In triple Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-; Ntn1β/β mutants, 20 out of 21 labeled axons have two branches.
source: while 20 out of 21 labeled axons in the triple Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-; Ntn1β/β mutants have two branches (Figure 4C and G).
evidence: This is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 4C and G.

claim: Neither Ntn1 nor Slit is required for the formation of two branches.
source: Since bifurcation remains nearly intact at this age for all these mutants, we conclude neither Ntn1 nor Slit is required for the formation of two branches.
evidence: This is concluded from the DiI labeling data showing similar bifurcation rates across all genotypes.

claim: In WT animals, the angle of bifurcation is on average 115.4°.
source: In WT animals, the angle of bifurcation is on average 115.4° (Figure 4H)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI labeled axons shown in Figure 4H.

claim: In WT animals, the average deviation is 10.2° and the difference between two angles from the same axons is 11.8°.
source: The average deviation is 10.2° (Figure 4I) and the difference between two angles from the same axons is 11.8 ° (Figure 4J)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI labeled axons shown in Figure 4I and J.

claim: In Slit1-/-;Slit2-/- mutant embryos, the average angle is 118.9°, the angle deviation is increased to 19.5° and the angle difference to 31.6°.
source: When analyzed together, the average angle is 118.9°, only marginally larger than WT (Figure 4H), but the angle deviation is increased to 19.5° and the angle difference to 31.6 ° (Figure 4I and J)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI labeled axons shown in Figure 4H, I and J.

claim: In Ntn1β/β mutant embryos, the average angle of bifurcation is ~108.0° with a deviation of 17.5° and a difference of 31.8°.
source: A similar angle difference was found in Ntn1β/β mutant embryos (Figure 4F). The average angle of bifurcation is ~108.0° (Figure 4H) with a deviation of 17.5° (Figure 4I) and a difference of 31.8°.
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI labeled axons shown in Figure 4H, I and J.

claim: In Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-; Ntn1β/β triple mutants, the average angle is 110.7°, and nearly all branches are deviated from the average angle by a margin of 37.8°.
source: Although the average angle is 110.7°, similar to that of WT (Figure 4H), nearly all branches are deviated from the average angle by a margin of 37.8°, significantly different from that seen in either Slit1;Slit2 or Ntn1 mutants (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI labeled axons shown in Figure 4H and I.

claim: The angle difference in triple mutants is increased dramatically, reaching 74.6°.
source: As a result, the angle difference is increased dramatically in the triple mutants, reaching 74.6° (Figure 4J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of DiI labeled axons shown in Figure 4J.

claim: The guidance of the two branches has different requirements of Ntn1 and Slit.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate the additive roles of Ntn1 and Slit, suggesting that the guidance of the two branches has different requirements of Ntn1 and Slit.
evidence: This is concluded from the quantitative analysis showing additive defects in triple mutants.

claim: DCC was previously shown to have a late-ingrowth defect.
source: we examined mice lacking the Ntn1 receptor DCC, which was previously shown to have a late-ingrowth defect
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on DCC mutant phenotypes.

claim: DCC is expressed at low levels in the DRG by in situ analysis.
source: DCC is expressed at low levels in the DRG by in situ analysis (Faure et al., 2020; Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work and in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Single cell RNAseq suggests DCC is expressed in a subset of sensory neurons.
source: and recent analysis by single cell RNAseq suggests DCC is expressed in a subset of sensory neurons
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous single cell RNAseq work.

claim: E10.5 Dcc mutants have similar misprojections as those in Ntn1 mutants.
source: Using wholemount analysis of E10.5 Dcc mutants, we found similar misprojections as those in Ntn1 mutants (Figure 5A and B, arrows).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Deletion of the Slit receptor Robo1 and Robo2 results in the same overshooting error as the loss of Slit1 and Slit2.
source: Since the deletion of the Slit receptor Robo1 and Robo2 results in the same overshooting error as the loss of Slit1 and Slit2
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on Robo mutant phenotypes.

claim: Robo1--/--;Robo2--/--;Dcc-/- triple mutants show extensive dorsal misprojections that fail to form axonal bundles of the dorsal funiculus.
source: Fluorescent labeling of sensory axons in E10.5 wholemount embryos reveals extensive dorsal misprojections that fail to form axonal bundles of the dorsal funiculus in the triple mutant when compared with the littermate control (Figure 5C and D).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount immunostaining data shown in Figure 5C and D.

claim: In Robo1-/-;Robo2--- mutant embryos, some fibers invade the spinal cord with straight trajectories that shoot horizontally in the dorsal spinal cord.
source: In Robo1-/-;Robo2--- mutant embryos (Figure 5G), , the DREZ still forms but some fibers invade the spinal cord with straight trajectories that shoot horizontally in the dorsal spinal cord (Figure 5I)
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 5G and I.

claim: In Dcc-/- only mutants, NF-labeled fibers misproject upward along the pial layer, leading to a reduced distance between the midline and the DREZ.
source: In Dcc-/- only mutants, the DREZ still forms and the NF-labeled fibers misproject upward along the pial layer (Figure 5F), leading to a reduced distance between the midline and the DREZ (Figure 5I)
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 5F and I.

claim: In Robo1--/--;Robo2--/--;Dcc-/- triple mutants, two types of misprojecting fibers are found, similar to those in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1β/β embryos.
source: In Robo1--/--;Robo2--/--;Dcc-/- triple mutants, two types of misprojecting fibers are found, similar to those in Slit1-/-;Slit2-/-;Ntn1β/β embryos (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by transverse section analysis shown in Figure 5H and comparison to Figure 3.

claim: Mice lacking either Robo1;Robo2 or DCC have similar total lengths of horizontal misprojections, but the triple mutants have increased total lengths.
source: When quantified, mice lacking either Robo1;Robo2 or DCC have similar total lengths of horizontal misprojections, but the triple mutants have increased total lengths, reflecting an increased number of misprojections (Figure 5J).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transverse sections shown in Figure 5J.

claim: The gap between the dorsal misprojections and the midline is reduced significantly in all receptor mutants.
source: In addition, the gap between the dorsal misprojections and the midline seems to be reduced significantly in all mutants (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis of transverse sections shown in Figure 5I.

claim: Loss of either the ligand or the receptor of both signaling systems has the same impact on DRG axon guidance at the DREZ.
source: These phenotypes are similar to those found in the analysis of Slit1;Slit2 and Ntn1 mutants above (Figure 3), thus demonstrating that loss of either the ligand or the receptor of both signaling systems has the same impact on DRG axon guidance at the DREZ.
evidence: This is concluded from the comparative analysis of ligand and receptor mutants.

claim: Development of the T-shaped structure requires both Ntn1 and Slit, which regulate different aspects of guidance during bifurcation.
source: We show that development of this stereotyped T-shaped structure requires both Ntn1 and Slit, which regulate different aspects of guidance during bifurcation.
evidence: This is concluded from the in vivo analysis of multiple mutant genotypes.

claim: Multiple mechanisms ensure the proper formation of the dorsal funiculus, a structure that is essential to sensory function in the mammalian spinal cord.
source: These results demonstrate the presence of multiple mechanisms to ensure the proper formation of the dorsal funiculus, a structure that is essential to sensory function in the mammalian spinal cord
evidence: This is concluded from the analysis showing additive defects in multiple mutants and is supported by citation to previous work on dorsal funiculus function.

claim: Loss of Ntn1 leads to a profound guidance error at the time of bifurcation, as misprojecting axons were found as early as E10.5, when the dorsal funiculus first forms.
source: However, our study showed that loss of this molecular pathway also leads to a profound guidance error at the time of bifurcation, as misprojecting axons were found as early as E10.5, when the dorsal funiculus first forms (Figure 1).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount and transverse section analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: The misprojecting axons in Ntn1 mutants do not stop at the DREZ but instead project more dorsally along the pial surface with random paths.
source: The misprojecting axons do not stop at the DREZ but instead project more dorsally along the pial surface with random paths
evidence: This is supported by wholemount and transverse section analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: Ntn1 is needed for proper guidance of DRG afferents right at the time when they bifurcate in the DREZ.
source: supporting the idea that Ntn1 is needed for proper guidance of DRG afferents right at the time when they bifurcate in the DREZ.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing and location of misprojections in Ntn1 mutants.

claim: Single axon DiI labeling at a later stage rules out the requirement of Ntn1 in bifurcation as the majority of DRG axons in Ntn1 mutants still form two branches.
source: Moreover, single axon DiI labeling at a later stage rules out the requirement of Ntn1 in bifurcation as the majority of DRG axons in Ntn1 mutants still form two branches (Figure 4).
evidence: This is supported by DiI labeling data shown in Figure 4.

claim: Both dorsal and medial misprojections were observed in recent studies of the embryo with complete Ntrn1 deletion, suggesting that Ntn1 may play multiple guidance roles.
source: Interestingly, both dorsal and medial misprojections were observed in the recent studies of the embryo with complete Ntrn1 deletion (Moreno-Bravo et al., 2019; Varadarajan and Butler, 2017; Wu et al., 2019), suggesting that Ntn1 may play multiple guidance roles.
evidence: This is inferred from citations to recent studies showing different types of misprojections in Ntn1 mutants.

claim: Ntn1 exerts its guidance function on DRG axons at the time of bifurcation.
source: Regardless, our single axon analysis (Figures 2 and 4) demonstrates that Ntn1 exerts its guidance function on DRG axons at the time of bifurcation.
evidence: This is concluded from the single axon analysis shown in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The guidance function of Ntn1 is supported by the similar defect found in mice lacking the Ntn1 receptor DCC.
source: The guidance function is further supported by the similar defect found in mice lacking the Ntn1 receptor DCC (Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount and transverse section analysis of DCC mutants shown in Figure 5.

claim: DCC function in DRG axons is reminiscent to that found in zebrafish DRG axons, which require proper DCC signaling to control actin-mediated invadopodia during the initial entry into the spinal cord.
source: This DCC function is reminiscent to that found in zebrafish DRG axons, which require proper DCC signaling to control actin-mediated invadopodia during the initial entry into the spinal cord
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on DCC function in zebrafish.

claim: Ntn1 proteins present locally outside the DREZ may provide a permissive cue that encourage the growth of newly bifurcated branches but restrict their trajectory within the DREZ.
source: One is that Ntn1 proteins present locally outside the DREZ (Figure 1—figure supplement 1; Serafini et al., 1996) provides a permissive cue that encourage the growth of newly bifurcated branches but restrict their trajectory within the DREZ
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on Ntn1 expression pattern and function.

claim: The permissive function of Ntn1 matches with the proposed adhesion function of DCC.
source: Such a permissive function matches with the proposed adhesion function of DCC
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on DCC adhesion function.

claim: The guidance function of Ntn1 may be mediated by a repulsive action, which can be mediated by both DCC and the repulsive receptor Unc5C.
source: Alternatively, it is possible that the guidance function is mediated by a repulsive action of Ntn1, which can be mediated by both DCC and the repulsive receptor Unc5C.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed based on receptor expression and in vitro data.

claim: Unc5C is expressed in DRG neurons.
source: This is supported by Unc5C expression in DRG neurons
evidence: This is stated as known information about Unc5C expression.

claim: Ntn1 has repulsive activity on E11.5 and E13.5 DRG axons in vitro.
source: as well as the repulsive activity of Ntn1 on E11.5 and E13.5 DRG axons in vitro
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: Ntn1 signaling plays a key role in DRG axon guidance right after bifurcation at the DREZ.
source: Regardless, our studies demonstrate a key role for Ntn1 signaling in DRG axon guidance right after bifurcation at the DREZ.
evidence: This is concluded from the in vivo analysis of Ntn1 and DCC mutants.

claim: There is complete disorganization and loss of axonal bundles in the dorsal funiculus when both Slit and Ntn1 pathways are impaired.
source: One striking result from our studies is the complete disorganization and the loss of axonal bundles in the dorsal funiculus when both Slit and Ntn1 pathways are impaired.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of triple mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: Nearly all DRG axons leave the DREZ and grow medially into the dorsal spinal cord in triple mutants lacking all three genes, Ntn1, Slit1, and Slit2.
source: This is reflected by the severe sensory misprojections in triple mutants lacking all three genes, Ntn1, Slit1, and Slit2, in which nearly all DRG axons leave the DREZ and grow medially into the dorsal spinal cord (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by wholemount and transverse section analysis of triple mutants shown in Figure 3.

claim: This is the first report of such a severe defect of the dorsal funiculus.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first report of such a severe defect of the dorsal funiculus.
evidence: This is stated as a novel finding based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: The guidance error found in Ntn1 mutants is different from that found in mice lacking Slit.
source: Importantly, when the misprojections were examined more carefully, we found that the guidance error found in Ntn1 mutants is different from that found in mice lacking Slit
evidence: This is concluded from the comparative analysis of misprojection trajectories in different mutants.

claim: The misprojections due to the loss of Slit signaling tend to enter the spinal cord horizontally whereas those from the loss of Ntn1/DCC grow more dorsally and stay at the pial surface.
source: The misprojections due to the loss of Slit signaling tend to enter the spinal cord horizontally whereas those from the loss of Ntn1/DCC grow more dorsally and stay at the pial surface (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of transverse sections shown in Figure 3.

claim: Misprojections in Slit/Robo mutants are relatively straight and horizontal whereas those in Ntn1 mutants are wavy and randomly oriented.
source: In addition, different growth trajectories were found for the misprojections: those in Slit/Robo mutants are relatively straight and horizontal whereas those in Ntn1 mutants are wavy and randomly oriented.
evidence: This is supported by comparative analysis of wholemount images shown in Figure 3.

claim: The misprojections seen in Slit/Robo mutants enter the spinal cord from the middle or the dorsal side of the DREZ, which is different from those medial misprojections found in Ntn1 mutants.
source: It is worth noting that the misprojections seen in Slit/Robo mutants enter the spinal cord from the middle or the dorsal side of the DREZ, which is different from those medial misprojections found in Ntn1 mutants discussed above
evidence: This is noted based on comparison with previous studies cited.

claim: Ntn1 and Slit have different actions in guiding DRG axons.
source: Nonetheless, these phenotypes suggest that Ntn1 and Slit have different actions in guiding DRG axons.
evidence: This is concluded from the different phenotypes observed in single and double mutants.

claim: Loss of both pathways results in added defects for both horizontally and dorsally invading misprojections.
source: Quantitative analysis shows that loss of both pathways results in added defects for both horizontally and dorsally invading misprojections (Figures 3—5)
evidence: This is supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figures 3-5.

claim: Slit and Ntn1 have non-redundant functions in DRG axon guidance.
source: suggesting non-redundant functions of the two mechanisms.
evidence: This is concluded from the additive defects observed in triple mutants.

claim: Slit and Ntn1 regulate branch guidance at two different steps during bifurcation: Slit guides the primary axon to turn into the DREZ, and Ntn1 regulates the trajectory of the two branches as they continue to grow along the DREZ.
source: we suggest that Slit and Ntn1 regulate branch guidance at two different steps during bifurcation (Figure 6). When the primary axon of DRG neurons first reach the dorsal spinal cord, they are guided by Slit to turn into the DREZ; after turning, the second branch is stimulated to form by CNP; and finally, the two branches continue to grow along the DREZ and their trajectory is regulated by Ntn1.
evidence: This is a model proposed based on the combined analysis of different mutants and is illustrated in Figure 6.

claim: Formation of a simple bifurcation structure requires multiple molecular mechanisms to ensure not only the formation of the second branches but also the correct orientation of both branches.
source: Altogether, our new study demonstrates that formation of a simple bifurcation structure requires multiple molecular mechanisms to ensure not only the formation of the second branches but also the correct orientation of both branches.
evidence: This is concluded from the comprehensive analysis of multiple mutants.

claim: The DREZ is an evolving structure that is not defined by any preexisting cell types.
source: However, in our view, the DREZ is an evolving structure that is not defined by any preexisting cell types.
evidence: This is a perspective proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: The DREZ is constructed at the location where DRG sensory axons first bifurcate, a process that involves the interaction of the DRG central axons with the cells in the dorsal spinal cord.
source: Rather, the DREZ is constructed at the location where DRG sensory axons first bifurcate, a process that involves the interaction of the DRG central axons with the cells in the dorsal spinal cord.
evidence: This is a perspective proposed by the authors based on their observations and previous studies.

claim: The growth cone of pioneer DRG sensory neurons uses actin-rich filopodia and invadopodia to interact with the glial environment and brake axon growth at the future DREZ.
source: This is best illustrated by the recent time-lapse imaging in the live zebrafish spinal cord, where the growth cone of pioneer DRG sensory neurons uses actin-rich filopodia and invadopodia to interact with the glial environment and brake axon growth at the future DREZ
evidence: This is supported by citations to recent live imaging studies in zebrafish.

claim: DCC signaling controls invadopodia stabilization during the precise guidance event of DRG axons entering the spinal cord.
source: Interestingly, DCC signaling was shown to control invadopodia stabilization during this precise guidance event
evidence: This is supported by citation to recent work on DCC function in zebrafish.

claim: Both formation of the second branch and guidance of both bifurcated branches are critical to establishing the DREZ.
source: Nonetheless, our identification of the role of extracellular cues like Slit, Ntn1, and CNP (Ma and Tessier-Lavigne, 2007; Zhao and Ma, 2009) supports the hypothesis that both formation of the second branch and guidance of both bifurcated branches are critical to establishing the DREZ.
evidence: This is concluded from the identification of multiple guidance cues and their roles.

claim: Sensory axon ingrowth and DREZ formation could be influenced by glial cells, especially boundary cap cells.
source: In addition to these extracellular cues, it has been suggested that sensory axon ingrowth and DREZ formation could be influenced by glial cells, especially boundary cap cells
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on boundary cap cells.

claim: Boundary cap cells are derived from late-born neural crest cells and associated with the dorsal root entry site starting at E12 in rat.
source: Since boundary cap cells are derived from late-born neural crest cells and associated with the dorsal root entry site starting at E12 in rat
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on boundary cap cell development.

claim: Boundary cap cells could potentially shape the DREZ during initial DRG axon ingrowth and bifurcation.
source: they could potentially shape the DREZ during initial DRG axon ingrowth and bifurcation.
evidence: This is speculated based on the timing and location of boundary cap cells.

claim: Boundary cap cells do not seem to correlate with growth of pioneer DRG axons to the DREZ in the developing zebrafish spinal cord.
source: Although boundary cap cells do not seem to correlate with growth of pioneer DRG axons to the DREZ in the developing zebrafish spinal cord
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work in zebrafish.

claim: Dorsal interneurons, which migrate ventrally at the time of DRG axon bifurcation, might play a role in DREZ formation.
source: Besides boundary cap cells, dorsal interneurons, which migrate ventrally at the time of DRG axon bifurcation, might also play a role here
evidence: This is speculated based on the timing of interneuron migration and their defects in mutants.

claim: Migration defects of dorsal interneurons have been reported in both Ntn1 and Dcc mutant embryos.
source: as migration defects have been reported in both Ntn1 and Dcc mutant embryos
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous work on interneuron migration defects.

claim: Dorsal interneurons could produce extracellular factors to control DRG axon guidance.
source: These cells could produce extracellular factors to control DRG axon guidance.
evidence: This is speculated based on the potential role of interneurons.

claim: Loss of TAG-1/Axonin-1 from dorsal interneurons causes similar but not identical afferent defects at the DREZ.
source: In fact, loss of TAG-1/Axonin-1 from these cells cause similar but not identical afferent defects at the DREZ
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work on TAG-1/Axonin-1 function.
